title: 4 Conversations That Defined ProcureCon Asia 2026
text: ProcureCon Asia wasn’t dominated by discussions about software, procurement suites, or the latest AI features. Instead, the conversations revolved around a more fundamental question: How is the role of procurement changing? Across keynotes and executive panels, procurement leaders consistently pointed to the same shift. Procurement is no longer expected to optimize purchasing alone, it is increasingly expected to influence business growth, innovation, resilience, and competitive advantage. Here are the four conversations that, in our view, defined this year’s conference. 1. Procurement Has Outgrown Being Measured as a Financial KPI Speaker: Dr. Prasanta Gupta Their emphasis: Procurement leaders should stop leading with cost savings and start demonstrating business impact: speed to market, resilience, innovation, and working capital. Procurement is becoming a boardroom function, not a back-office service. What this says about the industry: The CPO is increasingly expected to influence business strategy, not just supplier negotiations. Where tech fits in: Technology has to measure and connect these outcomes across procurement, finance, operations, and engineering - not just report purchase price variance. If your system’s dashboard still stops at “dollars saved,” it’s reporting on a KPI the best procurement leaders have already moved past. 2. Suppliers Should Become Innovation Partners Speaker: Elaine Chen Their emphasis: Supplier relationships are evolving beyond sourcing. Leading manufacturers are involving strategic suppliers earlier to improve design, manufacturability, and innovation, rather than engaging them only after requirements are finalized. What this says about the industry: Competitive advantage increasingly comes from the supplier ecosystem. Where tech fits in: Procurement systems must support continuous collaboration, not just transactional buying. A platform built purely for POs and invoices can’t support a supplier who’s effectively co-developing your next product. 3. Technology Is Not the Moat, Teams That Can Evolve With Technology Are Speakers: Terence Lee & Tomas Veit Their emphasis: Digital transformation succeeds when procurement changes how it works, not simply what software it buys. The operating model, governance, and cross-functional collaboration determine whether transformation scales. What this says about the industry: The biggest challenge is organizational, not technical. Where tech fits in: Technology should reinforce the operating model by connecting people, decisions, and workflows, instead of becoming another silo bolted onto an already fragmented stack. 4. AI Is Not Here to Help You Do Your Work, It’s Here to Do Your Work Speaker: Harendra Saksena Their emphasis: The discussion wasn’t “should we use AI?” but “how do we operationalize AI safely?” Governance, trust, and execution were recurring themes rather than experimentation. What this says about the industry: The conversation has moved from AI adoption to AI accountability. Where tech fits in: The next generation of procurement platforms will be judged by whether AI can execute real work reliably, not by how well it answers prompts. The Thread Connecting All Four Strip away the panel titles and one pattern runs through all four conversations. Procurement is being asked to operate at a higher altitude. Look for strategic impact instead of savings, embedded partnership instead of transactions, adaptive teams instead of one-time software purchases, and AI that executes instead of AI that merely assists. None of these shifts exist in isolation. But together, they redefine what procurement is expected to do. And for manufacturers, this isn't a future trend, it's today's operating reality. Multi-tier supplier networks, thin margins, and capital-intensive sourcing mean manufacturers feel every one of these shifts more intensely than others. You don’t want to run this reality on spreadsheets, email threads, disconnected ERPs and dashboards. That’s the real takeaway from ProcureCon Asia this year: Not whether manufacturers need modern procurement technology. But how fast can they close the gap, and whether their teams can keep closing it as the bar keeps moving. title: Manufacturing Has Gone Smart. Procurement Still Has Catching Up to Do
text: Last week, I attended INTEC 2026 in Coimbatore, one of India’s largest manufacturing and industrial trade exhibitions. The event brought together manufacturers, technology providers, machine builders, automation companies, and industrial leaders from across the country. Walking through the exhibition halls, you could feel the momentum. Smart machines, robotics, IoT-enabled systems, AI-powered applications, and advanced manufacturing technologies were everywhere. Indian manufacturing is clearly embracing digital transformation and preparing for a more connected, data-driven future. Yet amid all the innovation on display, one theme repeatedly surfaced in conversations with manufacturing leaders. Procurement remains one of the most overlooked areas of digital transformation. #1: Procurement Is Still Surprisingly Manual Across discussions with manufacturers from automotive, engineering, fabrication, industrial equipment, and textile sectors, a common challenge emerged. Supplier discovery still relies heavily on personal networks and past relationships. RFQs are often exchanged through lengthy email chains. Vendor information is scattered across spreadsheets, shared drives, and individual employees’ knowledge. Supplier evaluations are difficult to standardize. Critical sourcing decisions frequently depend on tribal knowledge rather than organizational intelligence. While manufacturing operations have become increasingly sophisticated, procurement processes often remain fragmented and reactive. The result is slower sourcing cycles, limited visibility, and increased operational risk. 💡 Takeaway: The shop floor has gone digital. The buying process feeding it hasn't. That gap is now a competitive liability. #2: The Knowledge Problem Is Bigger Than the Process Problem One of the most interesting observations was that many organizations don’t simply struggle with procurement workflows — they struggle with procurement knowledge. Who sourced this supplier before? Why was Vendor A selected over Vendor B? Which suppliers performed well on previous projects? Who within the organization has experience buying this category? In many companies, the answers exist — but only in someone’s inbox or someone’s memory. When employees leave, years of supplier intelligence leave with them. Organizations then spend time rediscovering information they already once knew. The hidden cost of procurement is often not purchasing itself — it’s the loss of institutional knowledge. 💡 Takeaway: Procurement isn't just a process problem. It's a knowledge retention problem. Every employee exit is also a supplier intelligence exit. #3: AI Has Moved Beyond Hype A few years ago, AI discussions at industrial events were largely exploratory. This year felt different. Manufacturers are no longer asking whether AI will impact their business. They’re asking where it can create the highest return. Across INTEC 2026, conversations centered around practical applications rather than futuristic possibilities. Leaders discussed predictive analytics for production planning, digital twins for factory simulation, real-time operational visibility, and AI-powered decision support systems. Procurement emerged as a particularly interesting area. Discussions ranged from generative AI for spend analysis and supplier intelligence to autonomous agents that can assist with supplier onboarding, RFQ management, and vendor qualification. Others spoke about machine learning models capable of predicting component demand weeks before traditional reorder points are triggered. What stood out was the shift in mindset. The focus is no longer on automation alone. Manufacturers are looking for systems that can augment decision-making, surface insights faster, and help teams act with greater confidence. In other words, the conversation has evolved from “How can we digitize this process?” to “How can we make better decisions?” 💡 Takeaway: AI at INTEC 2026 wasn’t a buzzword — it was a business case. The question on every leader’s mind was ROI, not possibility. #4: Procurement Is Becoming a Strategic Function Traditionally, procurement was viewed as a cost-control function. Today, manufacturers increasingly recognize that procurement directly influences operational resilience, production continuity, supplier innovation, and competitive advantage. The ability to find the right supplier quickly, evaluate alternatives effectively, and make informed sourcing decisions has become a strategic capability. As supply chains become more complex and market conditions become less predictable, procurement teams are being asked to contribute far more than purchase orders. They are being asked to drive business outcomes. 💡 Takeaway: Procurement has graduated from cost centre to strategic function. Companies that treat it as the former are leaving resilience — and margin — on the table. Where Slooze Fits In Many manufacturers have invested heavily in modernizing their shop floors. Fewer have invested in modernizing how they discover suppliers, manage sourcing knowledge, and make procurement decisions. This is the gap Slooze was built to solve. Slooze combines supplier discovery, procurement knowledge, sourcing workflows, and AI-powered intelligence into a single platform. Instead of relying on scattered spreadsheets, disconnected vendor databases, and individual employee expertise, procurement teams can access a centralized system that helps them find suppliers faster, preserve organizational knowledge, and make more confident sourcing decisions. The goal isn’t to replace procurement professionals. It’s to make every procurement professional exponentially more effective. Final Thought My biggest takeaway from INTEC 2026 wasn’t about robotics, automation, or AI. It was about the growing realization that manufacturing transformation extends beyond the factory floor. The companies that will lead the next decade of manufacturing won’t simply have smarter machines. They’ll have smarter systems, smarter decisions, and smarter procurement. And that journey is only beginning. Thanks for reading Slooze's newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and updates. title: Climbing the Procure-Tech Value Pyramid: India Insights
text: Enterprise procurement has long faced challenges : fragmented supplier ecosystems, manual workflows, inconsistent sourcing practices, limited spend visibility, and lengthy approval cycles. As organizations grow, these inefficiencies scale with them, driving significant operational costs. This is often the initial trigger for adopting procurement technology - solving an urgent pain point. Yet what enterprises quickly discover is that the benefits extend far beyond efficiency. Modern procure‑tech delivers deeper impact : it enhances organizational agility, strengthens governance, and unlocks profitability. An analysis of transformation initiatives at companies such as Havells, India Nippon Electricals, Pulcra Chemicals, Signature Global, and Gopal Snacks reveals a consistent journey of value creation. The Three Stages of Procure‑Tech Value Quick Wins - Immediate relief from inefficiencies and faster execution. Compounded Gains - Sustained improvements that multiply over time. Strategic Advantages - Procurement evolves into a driver of competitive edge. Organizations that successfully progress through all three stages elevate procurement from a back‑office support function into a true source of competitive advantage. 1. Quick Wins: The Immediate ROI These are the outcomes that typically justify the investment. They appear within weeks or months and are usually measurable. a) Faster Procurement Cycles One of the first improvements organizations experience is a reduction in sourcing and approval timelines. Signature Global reported a 30–40% reduction in PR-to-PO cycle times after digitizing procurement workflows. By eliminating manual approvals, email-based coordination, and fragmented documentation, procurement teams can execute sourcing events significantly faster. Business Impact Faster project execution Reduced operational bottlenecks Improved procurement responsiveness b) Immediate Cost Savings Digital sourcing introduces supplier competition, structured bidding, and better price discovery. Examples include: Gopal Snacks achieving ₹7.3 crore in savings Noon reporting approximately $7 million in savings Emami realizing annual savings of 8–10% Logistics procurement programs delivering 15–20% savings Business Impact Lower procurement costs Better budget utilization Immediate contribution to profitability c) Increased Transparency Organizations quickly gain visibility into: Spend Suppliers Procurement status Negotiation history Approval workflows This transparency often becomes the foundation for every future improvement. 2. Compounded Gains: The Benefits That Grow Over Time Unlike cost savings, these outcomes accumulate month after month. The longer the platform is used, the more valuable it becomes. a) Better Supplier Ecosystems Companies such as Pulcra Chemicals and Havells used digital procurement platforms to standardize supplier engagement and sourcing processes. Over time this creates: Higher supplier participation Stronger vendor relationships Better supplier performance Increased sourcing competition Every sourcing event generates more data and strengthens procurement intelligence. Business Impact A stronger supplier ecosystem produces better pricing and improved supply reliability year after year. b) Procurement Intelligence As sourcing events accumulate, organizations begin building proprietary procurement knowledge. Teams can identify: High-performing suppliers Cost trends Category benchmarks Savings opportunities Negotiation patterns What begins as software gradually becomes an organizational intelligence asset. Business Impact Better sourcing decisions Improved forecasting Reduced procurement risk c) Compliance and Governance Organizations such as India Nippon Electricals and Kwality Group reported improved compliance visibility and audit readiness. The value compounds because every sourcing event creates: Audit trails Approval histories Supplier records Negotiation documentation Compliance becomes embedded into the process rather than added afterward. Business Impact Reduced audit effort Lower governance risk Improved procurement discipline 3. Strategic Wins: Procurement as a Competitive Advantage This is where procurement technology begins influencing business outcomes beyond procurement itself. The discussion shifts from savings to growth. a) Procurement Becomes a Strategic Function When procurement leaders gain visibility into spend, suppliers, contracts, and market dynamics, they become strategic advisors to the business. Instead of asking: “How do we buy cheaper?” Organizations begin asking: “How do we source smarter?” Business Impact Better capital allocation Improved supplier strategy Stronger decision-making b) Increased Organizational Agility Modern enterprises operate in volatile supply environments. Organizations with digitized procurement functions can: Source alternatives faster Respond to disruptions quicker Scale supplier networks efficiently Adapt sourcing strategies rapidly This agility becomes increasingly valuable during periods of uncertainty. Business Impact Greater resilience Faster response to market changes Reduced supply chain disruption c) Revenue Growth and Business Expansion The most advanced procurement organizations eventually influence revenue. One documented food manufacturing case reported approximately ₹60 crore in revenue growth after procurement optimization improved sourcing responsiveness and operational scalability. This demonstrates a critical shift: Procurement is no longer solely a cost-management function. It becomes an enabler of business growth. Business Impact Faster market expansion Improved operational capacity Higher revenue potential Closing Notes As we’ve seen from the examples above, procurement technology consistently delivers measurable outcomes: multi‑crore savings double‑digit cost reductions faster sourcing cycles improved compliance visibility stronger supplier participation documented revenue growth This is true across industries - manufacturing, chemicals, construction, retail and similar. Enterprises that embrace modern Procure-Tech unlock value far beyond short‑term efficiency gains. The journey from Quick Wins to Compounded Gains and ultimately Strategic Advantages demonstrates how procurement can evolve into a true growth engine. In the long term, organizations that treat procurement technology as a core infrastructure layer - rather than just an operational tool, position themselves for resilience, profitability, and competitive advantage. The evidence is clear: procure‑tech is not simply about saving costs, but about transforming procurement into a strategic capability that drives enterprise success.

title: 5 Questions to Ask Your Procurement Tech Vendor (Before You Sign Anything)
text: This article is for people who are in following stages of awareness ( in BOLD ) Un → Problem → SOLUTION → PRODUCT → Most You know you have a procurement problem. And You’re reacting to risks debating your savings bypassing key stakeholders Your best people are buried inside systems decisions are gut-advised technology makes you work on it, not the other way way around If you're not already familiar with the term: Value-Maxing is the new cool. And in procurement, that potential is enormous and mostly untapped. So this is your guide to Value-Maxing your investment in Procurement Tech. Here’s the honest reality of what happens next: vendors will line up to show you a slick demo, echo the AI movement, and hand you slide decks full of generic ROI claims. That’s the game. We know, we play it too. But we’re also here to do something different. We want to help you ask the right questions. The ones that move the conversation beyond surface-level promises and into what actually matters - domain complexity, supplier experience, practical AI, proactive risk intelligence, and real time-to-value. Because the goal isn’t to be impressed in a demo room. The goal is to avoid regret six months after you sign. Turn an impression into action. Here are the five questions that do it. Q1: How complex can the platform get? and how deeply does it connect to our existing systems? Why this matters: You need to know if the platform can handle your real-world procurement complexity, not just simple POs. And you need to know whether it talks to your ERP or becomes yet another silo your team has to maintain alongside everything else. A lightweight tool works for a 50-person company. You need a platform that handles messy reality . Dig into: Can it handle multi-category, multi-plant, multi-currency sourcing events simultaneously? Does it integrate natively with SAP, Oracle, or your ERP or via workarounds? What happens to data that lives in your ERP today - does it sync, migrate, or co-exist? Can approval hierarchies and spend limits from our ERP be respected inside the platform? What to listen for: A live demo, Ask them to walk through the PR-to-PO flow end to end. If they can’t do it in the demo, they can’t do it in your business. This question separates enterprise-grade platforms from tools that work well in a pilot and fall apart at scale. Q2: Walk me through exactly what my supplier sees, shares, and does on this platform. Why this matters: A procurement platform is only as powerful as supplier participation. If the platform is painful for your vendors - clunky, confusing or time-consuming, their adoption collapses and so does your competitive leverage. You might not be in the best position if only two suppliers show up. Great platforms treat suppliers as co-users Dig into: What does supplier onboarding look like - how long, how much effort on their side? Can suppliers see their own performance scores, payment status, and open pending work in one place? How do suppliers submit quotes, documents, and compliance certificates? Can they update it? Is the portal mobile-friendly - especially for smaller vendors who work off a phone? What to listen for: Ask for a live supplier engagement walkthrough. The best vendors will show you both sides of the screen in a single demo - buyer view and supplier view. If they only show you the buyer side, ask why. This is the question most buyers skip and the one they regret most after go-live. Q3: Show me how AI actually works in the platform, not the pitch, the real thing, and how it impacts or benefits my team Why this matters: Every vendor says “AI-powered” and the gap between marketing & reality is legit. But a very few can show you AI catch patterns, suggest decisions, surface insights, or save work-hours, in a live walkthrough. You don’t need AI for the sake of it Dig into: Where exactly does AI intervene: sourcing, vendor scoring, spend analysis, contract review? Does AI make recommendations or take autonomous actions - and can we control which? How does the system learn from our historical data over time? What does a day in the life of my procurement team look like with AI vs without it on this platform? What to listen for: A concrete before/after. Not “AI reduces maverick spend”. Specificity is everything here. here’s the alert your team would have seen last Tuesday before that off-contract purchase happened. here's a cluster of invoices from the same supplier showing the same overcharge pattern across three different POs. Your team would never see this manually. A vendor who can answer this well will make your team genuinely excited about using the platform. That matters more than you think. Q4: Give me a real example of how the platform helps us act before something goes wrong, find savings we’re leaving on the table, and plan smarter. Why this matters: This is the “show, don’t tell” question. You’re not asking about features - you’re asking them to demonstrate intelligence. A great vendor will light up here. An average one will go back to the slides. Dig into: There are three things you’re really asking about: Proactive risk: How does the platform flag a supplier concentration risk, delivery delay pattern, or compliance gap before it becomes an incident? Not after the supply chain breaks - before. Cost gaps: How does spend analytics surface that you’re paying 18% above benchmark in a category - and what action does it suggest? Can it show you where consolidating two suppliers into one would improve your negotiating position? Procurement strategy: Can the platform help  you decide when to run an e-auction vs negotiate directly vs lock in a long-term contract? Does it give your CPO a strategic view - not just an operational one? What to listen for: Real examples from real clients, not hypotheticals. If they can name the outcome - “a client in your sector avoided a ₹2 crore supply disruption because the platform flagged a single-source dependency six weeks before the disruption” - that’s a vendor who understands value. If they can’t, they’re still selling you software. This question tests intelligence, not just functionality. It’s also the one that will surprise you in the room - because most vendors aren’t prepared for it. Q5: How long does it take to go live? Does it disrupt our existing flows? And when can I see my first dollar of value added? Why this matters: The hidden cost of procurement technology isn’t the contract/agreement. A vendor’s "Go-live in 12 weeks" often means: 12 weeks to sign the contract, 12 more weeks of implementation, 12 more weeks of testing, and then you realize you it’s six months of internal disruption, change management, and organizational patience - with no ROI in sight. You need straight answers on three things: time, disruption, and value . Dig into: What is the realistic go-live timeline - and what does your team need to do vs what they handle? Does rollout happen in parallel with our current process, or do we have to switch over fully? What’s the first workflow that will be live - and what savings or efficiency gain comes with it? How soon after go-live have comparable clients seen measurable impact? What to listen for: A phased plan with clear milestones and a committed “first value” moment — ideally within the first 30 days of go-live, not six months in. If they can’t tell you when you’ll see the first rupee of impact, they don’t have enough skin in the game. The best vendors will offer to co-own the outcomes. They’ll propose a success framework, name the KPIs they’ll track with you, and want to be held accountable at 30, 60, and 90 days. How to use these five questions These aren’t interrogation tactics - they’re conversation starters. Use them to shift the dynamic from a vendor presentation to a genuine working session. The best procurement tech relationships start with a vendor who welcomes hard questions, not one who deflects them. If a vendor can answer all five well you’ve probably found someone worth working with. If they can’t, you’ve saved yourself six months of the wrong answer. title: Procurement’s toughest battle aren't with your vendors, It’s with your own team.
text: Figure 1: A picture showcasing how teams collaborate in ‘Procurement’ The Convoluted Nature of Procurement Procurement looks deceptively simple from the outside: find a supplier, negotiate a price, sign a contract. In reality, it’s a convoluted, multi‑level, multi‑tier collaboration nightmare. You don’t just buy a product—you manage a web of stakeholders with competing priorities. Business teams define the need, sourcing runs the process, operations cares about delivery, compliance watches for risk, and tech has system limits no one warned you about. Procurement professionals live their jobs in the “in‑between” spaces, chasing signatures, reconciling conflicting requirements, and navigating a constant maze of dependencies and approvals. And no, you cannot solve this by simply putting everyone in a room for one meeting—procurement is a living, breathing process that demands continuous alignment. Figure 1: A picture showcasing how teams collaborate in ‘Procurement’ Share Power, Politics, and the Pain of Influence We’ve spent billions building sophisticated tools to engage with vendors—RFx platforms, SRM portals, auction software—yet almost nothing exists to help us work internally. Instead, procurement teams rely on a fragile cocktail of Slack pings, endless email threads, and “quick” WhatsApp messages. These tools are fine for transmitting information, but they fail at true collaboration; they don’t hold project context, and they force us back into the grind of status meetings just to keep everyone aligned. The result is a fragmented, fragile system where procurement leads spend more time influencing and coordinating stakeholders than actually sourcing, holding the process together through sheer grit rather than structured mechanisms. The Role & Engagement Debate Procurement needs every function to work together, but not all at once. The paradox is that when everyone piles in simultaneously, you get role overlap and “too many cooks.” When they’re absent, you get a “not my problem” attitude. The result is constant clashes over ownership, delegation, and reporting lines that slow down the process and create risk. Business → should engage early to define needs, then step back. Compliance → must be embedded continuously, not bolted on at the end. Tech → should raise constraints before the RFP, not after the vendor is chosen. Operations → needs to validate delivery capability, not just accept a handover. And nowhere is the dysfunction more damaging than with compliance. Ideally, risk and governance are woven into the team’s DNA from day one. In reality, compliance is often treated as an afterthought—surfacing only after the purchase order is signed or during a painful yearly audit. By then, the wrong supplier is already in place. The bad contract is already signed. The risk is already live. Your Tools Aren’t Wrong, Your Problem Is The issue isn’t that procurement tools are inadequate—it’s that the real problem lies in how teams collaborate. Rethinking procurement means shifting focus from external negotiations to internal alignment. The bottleneck isn’t the supplier; it’s the 7 to 13 people inside the building who can’t agree on what they want. You are not failing because your tools are bad. You are not failing because you need a better contract repository. You are failing because you’re trying to solve an internal alignment problem with external vendor tools. Those tools assume the hard part is the supplier. But in industrial and manufacturing procurement, the hard part is aligning business, ops, compliance, and tech before the RFP ever leaves the building. That means building a workflow for internal agreement—a single source of truth for constraints, non‑negotiables, and handoffs. Because once your team is aligned, the vendor conversation becomes straightforward. Almost easy. The vendor was never the problem. The other 12 people in the room were. Where Slooze Fits In Procurement has always been treated as a vendor problem—better RFPs, smarter auctions, tighter contracts. But the real bottleneck isn’t outside your walls, it’s inside them. The hardest part of procurement is aligning the 7 to 13 stakeholders who all have different priorities, constraints, and veto power. That’s why we built Slooze : not to replace your vendor tools, but to solve the internal alignment problem they were never designed to fix. Slooze provides the connective tissue procurement teams have been missing. It creates a structured workflow where business, operations, compliance, finance, and tech can align before the RFP ever leaves the building. By embedding collaboration into the process, Slooze transforms procurement from a battle of influence into a streamlined, cooperative effort.
